name: Lisbon
note: Getting expensive. D8 visa required. Best Apr–Jun & Sep–Oct.
description: Portugal's capital spreads over steep hills at the mouth of the Tagus, its miradouros (viewpoints) looking across rooftops to the river. It is Europe's second-oldest capital after Athens, and much of the centre was rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. Living here for a month is neighbourhood-scale: a cappuccino for about €2.70, a cheap lunch near €15, errands on foot. The metro's four lines and six tram lines, including the 28, cover the centre; a monthly pass is about €40. Coworkings such as Second Home, Heden and Factory Lisbon charge roughly €180–250 a month for a hot desk. Fibre at 200–500 Mbps is common, though parts of Alfama lack it. Clocks follow WET/WEST, like London, and Portugal offers a digital nomad visa. The climate is Mediterranean: mild, rainy winters with January highs of 14–19°C and dry summers reaching 25–32°C in August. With about 2,875 sunshine hours a year, spring and autumn are the easiest seasons. Trade-offs: a central one-bedroom rents for about €1,425 a month after years of rising rents, the stone calçada gets slippery on steep streets, and the busiest districts are crowded with visitors.

neighbourhoods.name: Príncipe Real
neighbourhoods.about: Hilltop streets of mansions, antique shops and a romantic garden
neighbourhoods.description: Príncipe Real sits on the hill next to Bairro Alto, between the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara and São Bento. Its centre is the Jardim do Príncipe Real, a romantic-style garden laid out in the mid-19th century around an octagonal pond and a huge Buçaco cedar. Visit Lisboa describes the area as a mix of grand mansions, small antique shops, restaurants and kiosks. Under the garden lies the 1864 Patriarcal reservoir, now part of the EPAL water museum, and an organic produce market is held there on Saturdays. It lies just outside the bar streets of Bairro Alto, so nightlife is a short walk away rather than under the window. It suits long stays, couples and travellers who want a central, upscale base.
watch_out: Hilltop location: most walks back from the river are uphill
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Rato (yellow line) metro is the nearest station; tram 24E runs through Príncipe Real between Chiado (Camões) and Campolide.

neighbourhoods.name: Bairro Alto
neighbourhoods.about: 16th-century grid of narrow lanes and Lisbon's main bar district
neighbourhoods.description: Bairro Alto grew outside the old city walls in the 16th century on an almost regular grid of streets. Its long, narrow three- and four-storey houses line lanes so tight that often only the upper floors get direct sun. By day the lanes are calmer, with alternative shops selling records and art, and hairdressers. At night the lanes fill with people drinking in the street, and Visit Lisboa calls it the centre of the city's nightlife; a typical night continues downhill to Bica and Cais do Sodré. Residents have complained for years about noise from bars and street drinking. It suits night owls and short stays; anyone needing sleep or a quiet place to work should look at Príncipe Real or Chiado next door.
watch_out: Loud late into the night, especially at weekends
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Baixa-Chiado (blue and green lines) metro is the nearest station; tram 28E passes along the edge at Chiado.

neighbourhoods.name: Intendente
neighbourhoods.about: Revived square off Almirante Reis with tiled façades and late bars
neighbourhoods.description: Intendente takes its name from the Largo do Intendente Pina Manique, a square off Avenida Almirante Reis in the former Anjos parish, now part of Arroios. Long run down, the square was rehabilitated in 2012. The square has the Art Nouveau 1908 Lisboa Hotel, the tiled façade of the old Viúva Lamego ceramics works and Casa Independente, a bar in an 1860s palace with live music. Around it are cafés, brunch spots, coworking spaces and an international food scene. Rents are among the lowest in central Lisbon and the green metro line runs underneath. It suits budget-minded long-stayers and creatives who prefer a lived-in area to a postcard one.
watch_out: Some streets toward Martim Moniz feel rough late at night
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Intendente, Anjos and Martim Moniz stations are all on the green line; tram 28E starts at Martim Moniz.

neighbourhoods.name: Chiado
neighbourhoods.about: Upmarket shopping streets, theatres and historic cafés
neighbourhoods.description: Chiado has been Lisbon's shopping and cultural quarter since the 18th and 19th centuries. A fire in 1988 destroyed 18 buildings; architect Álvaro Siza Vieira led the rebuild, which kept the old façades and added the Baixa-Chiado metro station. Daily life centres on Rua Garrett and Praça Luís de Camões, with designer shops, pavement cafés such as A Brasileira, the Bertrand bookshop (opened 1747), the São Carlos opera house and the Chiado Museum. It is busy with visitors during the day. Chiado sits between Bairro Alto and the flat Baixa, so nightlife is close without being outside the door. It suits luxury travellers and anyone who wants to walk to most sights.
watch_out: Crowded with visitors during the day
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Baixa-Chiado (blue and green lines) metro; trams 28E and 24E stop at Praça Luís de Camões.

neighbourhoods.name: Alfama
neighbourhoods.about: Lisbon's oldest quarter of steep alleys, viewpoints and fado houses
neighbourhoods.description: Alfama is Lisbon's oldest neighbourhood, on the slope between the Castelo de São Jorge and the Tagus. Its name comes from the Arabic for hot springs, and because the 1755 earthquake largely spared it, it keeps a medieval maze of lanes and small squares. Visit Lisboa describes cobbled alleys with steep inclines, fado houses and viewpoints such as Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol. The Sé cathedral, São Vicente de Fora and the National Pantheon are nearby, and tram 28E climbs through it. Many houses have been renovated and fado restaurants have opened. It suits travellers who want atmosphere and views and do not mind stairs; carrying luggage up the lanes takes effort.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Santa Apolónia and Terreiro do Paço (blue line) are the nearest metro stations; trams 28E and 12E run through the quarter.

neighbourhoods.name: Baixa
neighbourhoods.about: Flat 18th-century grid between Rossio and the river
neighbourhoods.description: The Baixa Pombalina is the grid of streets rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake under the Marquis of Pombal, running from Praça do Comércio on the river to Rossio and Praça da Figueira. Its buildings were among the first designed to resist earthquakes. It is flat, pedestrianised in parts and the easiest area of the centre to walk. Rua Augusta and the side streets are lined with traditional shops, patisseries, souvenir shops and restaurants, and the area is busy with visitors from morning to evening. Three metro lines and several tram routes meet here, so it works as a base for short stays and first visits. Visit Lisboa calls it the city's best-known area, so it is rarely quiet in the daytime.
watch_out: Crowded tourist streets; pickpockets on busy trams and metro
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Rossio (green), Restauradores and Terreiro do Paço (blue) and Baixa-Chiado (blue and green) metro stations; trams 12E, 15E, 25E and 28E.

neighbourhoods.name: Cais do Sodré
neighbourhoods.about: Riverside transport hub with a food hall and the bars of Pink Street
neighbourhoods.description: Cais do Sodré is a stretch of Lisbon's central waterfront. Known as Bairro dos Remolares in the early 19th century, it was rebuilt from 1855 with warehouses and port businesses, and Eça de Queirós set scenes of Os Maias in its Hotel Central. Today the Mercado da Ribeira is a large food hall, and at night the bars and clubs of Rua Nova do Carvalho, known as Pink Street, stay open late. Trains to Cascais, ferries across the Tagus to Cacilhas and the green metro line all leave from here. It suits night owls and travellers planning day trips along the river to Belém and Cascais. Residents have complained about late-night noise and street drinking.
watch_out: Loud bar crowds late at night around Pink Street
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Cais do Sodré (green line) metro, trains to Cascais, ferries to Cacilhas and trams 15E and 18E.

neighbourhoods.name: Avenidas Novas
neighbourhoods.about: Wide avenues, offices and the Gulbenkian north of the old centre
neighbourhoods.description: Avenidas Novas is the civil parish named after Lisbon's expansion northward in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when new avenues were laid across farmland. The current parish was created in 2012 from Nossa Senhora de Fátima and São Sebastião da Pedreira. It is a modern district of apartment blocks, offices and high-rises along wide avenues, with plenty of cafés and restaurants. The Calouste Gulbenkian Museum and its park, the Campo Pequeno bullring and the Galveias Palace are here. Three metro lines meet here, and the red line reaches the airport in about 16 minutes from Saldanha. It suits remote workers on long stays who want newer buildings and an everyday city rather than a historic one.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Saldanha (yellow and red), São Sebastião (blue and red), Picoas and Campo Pequeno (yellow) metro stations.

best_season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct (warm, fewer crowds). Jul–Aug is hot and packed; winter is mild but rainy.
time_zone: UTC+0/+1 with daylight saving — about 5h ahead of US Eastern.
sim_cost: MEO or NOS ≈ $15–20/mo (15–30 GB); eSIMs run ≈ $10. Coverage excellent.
english_level: Widely spoken — among the best in southern Europe.
getting_around: Metro, trams and trains cover the city; Uber and Bolt are cheap. Hills are real.
scene: Enormous — one of the top nomad capitals in the world, endless meetups and coworkings.

name: Porto
note: Less touristy than Lisbon. More authentic. Growing nomad scene.
description: Portugal's second city climbs steep granite slopes above the Douro estuary, facing the port wine lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia across the river. Its historic centre, with the Dom Luís I Bridge, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. A month here is affordable by Western European standards: a cappuccino costs about €2.40 and a cheap meal about €12. The metro's six lines meet at Trindade, and an Andante Metropolitano pass covering metro, buses and urban trains costs €40 a month. Coworkings include CRU (about €60–140 a month) and Porto i/o (€40–200). Portugal's median fixed broadband is about 360 Mbps (Ookla, August 2026). Clocks follow WET/WEST, like London, and Portugal offers a digital nomad visa. The climate is mild Atlantic-Mediterranean: January highs near 14°C, August highs near 26°C. Rain totals about 1,240 mm a year, mostly from October to April, so May to September is the most reliable stretch. Trade-offs: a central one-bedroom rents for about €1,150 a month, the hills and stairs between the river and the centre are tiring, and the Ribeira and Baixa fill with visitors in summer.

neighbourhoods.name: Ribeira
neighbourhoods.about: Riverfront quarter of the old town, facing the Gaia wine lodges
neighbourhoods.description: Ribeira is one of the oldest parts of Porto, in the former parish of São Nicolau on the Douro, and lies inside the historic centre that UNESCO listed in 1996. Today its riverside is lined with bars and restaurants and draws large numbers of visitors. Its landmarks are the Praça da Ribeira, the Rua da Fonte Taurina, one of the city's oldest streets, the Muro dos Bacalhoeiros and the Casa do Infante, where Prince Henry the Navigator is believed to have been born in 1394. Wikivoyage notes that its bars usually close around 03:00–04:00. It suits short stays and first-time visitors who want the river view, less so anyone who needs quiet evenings or level streets.
watch_out: Crowded with visitors, especially in summer
Steep streets and stairs up to the centre
neighbourhoods.getting_around: The Funicular dos Guindais climbs from Ribeira to Batalha, heritage tram 1 runs along the river to Foz, and São Bento station is uphill.

neighbourhoods.name: Baixa
neighbourhoods.about: Downtown Porto around Avenida dos Aliados, Bolhão and São Bento
neighbourhoods.description: Baixa is Porto's downtown, the area of banks, shops and services around the Avenida dos Aliados, whose construction began in 1916 and which ends at the City Hall. Rua de Santa Catarina, the Bolhão market and São Bento station, known for its azulejo panels, are all here. The area lost residents for decades as buildings decayed; the Porto Vivo urban rehabilitation company was set up in 2004 and many buildings have since been restored. The Bolhão market reopened in full after a major refurbishment. Torre dos Clérigos (226 steps) and Livraria Lello, which now sells timed tickets, sit on its western edge. It is the most practical base for a long stay, with metro stations on every side.
watch_out: Livraria Lello and Clérigos draw long queues
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Aliados and São Bento stations serve metro line D, Bolhão and Trindade serve lines A, B, C, E and F, and São Bento has suburban trains.

neighbourhoods.name: Cedofeita
neighbourhoods.about: Shopping street, Romanesque church and Porto's gallery quarter
neighbourhoods.description: Cedofeita is a former parish just west of downtown, with about 22,000 residents in 2011 on 2.7 km². Its namesake street, Rua de Cedofeita, is a long pedestrian shopping street, and the small Romanesque Igreja de São Martinho de Cedofeita stands on the Largo do Priorado. Rua de Miguel Bombarda, a 650-metre street running from Rua de Cedofeita towards Massarelos, holds several dozen art galleries that open their new shows on the same Saturday each month, drawing crowds. It is mostly residential, with cafés and independent shops, and sits within walking distance of Baixa. It suits long stays and remote workers who want a central base that is calmer than the riverfront.
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Trindade, the hub of all metro lines, is a short walk east, and Lapa and Carolina Michaëlis stations serve lines A, B, C, E and F.

neighbourhoods.name: Bonfim
neighbourhoods.about: Old industrial parish east of downtown, now residential, on the metro
neighbourhoods.description: Bonfim is a parish east of downtown with about 23,000 residents on 3 km² (2021 census). It was carved out of Santo Ildefonso, Campanhã and Sé, and its limits were fixed in 1956. It was an industrial parish, and some old factories still stand, most now closed; today trade, banking and services dominate. Its heritage includes the Porto Municipal Public Library, the Arca de Água de Mijavelhas and the Igreja do Bonfim, built between 1874 and 1894. Rents are lower here than in Baixa or Foz, and the metro reaches downtown in a few stops. It suits long stays on a budget and travellers who prefer a local neighbourhood to the tourist core.
watch_out: Farther from the river and old-town sights than Baixa
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Campo 24 de Agosto and Heroísmo stations serve metro lines A, B, C, E and F, a few stops from Bolhão and Trindade.

neighbourhoods.name: Boavista
neighbourhoods.about: Business district along the avenue from the Rotunda to the sea
neighbourhoods.description: Boavista is not a parish but the area along the nearly 6.8 km axis of Rua and Avenida da Boavista, from Praça da República to the Atlantic. The name is used most for the area around the Praça de Mouzinho de Albuquerque, known as the Rotunda da Boavista. Rem Koolhaas's Casa da Música concert hall, opened in 2005, stands by the Rotunda. Farther west lies the Serralves Foundation, a contemporary art museum by Álvaro Siza with a large park, and Boavista FC's Estádio do Bessa is nearby. Offices, shopping centres and larger hotels line the avenue. It suits business travellers and long stays that value modern flats and transport over old-town character.
watch_out: Long avenue: the western end is a bus or drive from downtown
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Casa da Música station serves metro lines A, B, C, E and F, and the MetroBus line 1 runs from there to Império since February 2026.

neighbourhoods.name: Foz do Douro
neighbourhoods.about: Upmarket seaside district where the Douro meets the Atlantic
neighbourhoods.description: Foz do Douro lies at the mouth of the Douro on Porto's western edge. It was briefly a separate town (1833–1836) before joining Porto; its oldest core, Foz Velha, runs roughly between Rua da Cerca and Rua da Beneditina. Known as an upper-class district, it has a seafront promenade with terraces, bars and gardens. The Forte de São João Baptista guards the river mouth, the Felgueiras pier ends in a 10-metre lighthouse, and the Cantareira chapel-lighthouse is an early Renaissance building. Wikivoyage lists the Michelin-starred Pedro Lemos and nightclubs such as Industria here. It suits couples and long stays that want sea air and walks, at the cost of a longer ride to the centre.
watch_out: Windier and cooler than the centre
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Heritage tram 1 runs along the river from Ribeira to Foz, and STCP bus 500 follows the riverfront and the ocean front.

neighbourhoods.name: Massarelos
neighbourhoods.about: Riverside slope below the Crystal Palace gardens, west of the centre
neighbourhoods.description: Massarelos is a former parish of about 1.9 km² on the north bank of the Douro, west of the historic centre; in 2013 it merged with Lordelo do Ouro. It climbs from the river up towards Boavista and the end of Rua de Miguel Bombarda. Its main green space is the Jardins do Palácio de Cristal, with views over the river towards the sea and the Rosa Mota pavilion at its centre. The Museu do Carro Eléctrico, opened in 1992 in the old Massarelos power station, keeps 16 historic trams. It is mostly residential and quieter than Ribeira, yet within walking distance of downtown. It suits long stays and travellers who want river views and a park nearby.
watch_out: Steep climb between the riverside and the gardens
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Heritage trams 1 and 18 and STCP bus 500 stop at the Museu do Carro Eléctrico on the riverfront.

neighbourhoods.name: Gaia Riverside
neighbourhoods.about: Port wine cellars and the best views of Porto, across the river
neighbourhoods.description: Vila Nova de Gaia is a separate municipality on the south bank of the Douro, facing Porto's historic centre. Its riverfront, the Cais de Gaia, was for centuries a river port that shipped port wine, and the wine cellars are still there. The current promenade of terraces, restaurants and bars was rebuilt between 2000 and 2003. Above it, the Jardim do Morro garden and the Serra do Pilar monastery, part of the UNESCO site, look across to the Ribeira, and the upper deck of the Dom Luís I Bridge carries walkers and the metro. Many cellars run guided tours and tastings. It suits short stays built around port wine and views, and travellers who prefer to look at the old town rather than sleep in it.
watch_out: Steep climb from the quay to Jardim do Morro
neighbourhoods.getting_around: Jardim do Morro station (metro line D) sits at the south end of the Dom Luís I Bridge's upper deck; the lower deck is a short walk to Ribeira.

best_season: May–Jun and Sep (warm, drier). Winters are wetter and cooler than Lisbon.
flight_from_miami: ≈9h via Lisbon, or seasonal direct flights ≈9h to OPO.
time_zone: UTC+0/+1 with daylight saving — about 5h ahead of US Eastern.
english_level: Good — widely understood in the centre and service jobs.
getting_around: Compact and walkable centre; metro to the airport and beach suburbs.
scene: Medium and growing — calmer and cheaper than Lisbon, still well-networked.

name: Ericeira
note: World Surfing Reserve. 40 min from Lisbon. Year-round surfable waves.
best_season: May–Oct for surf and sun (Sep–Oct is the sweet spot). Winters are mild but stormy, with the biggest swells.
flight_from_miami: ≈8h direct to Lisbon (LIS), then 45 min by car or bus.
time_zone: UTC+0/+1 with daylight saving — about 5h ahead of US Eastern.
sim_cost: MEO or NOS ≈ $15–20/mo; coverage good in town.
english_level: Good — the surf scene runs largely in English.
getting_around: Walkable village; a car or scooter unlocks the surf breaks up and down the coast.
scene: Small and surf-led — digital nomad surfers cluster around a few cowork/co-live spaces.
